#8263. Weekend Warm-Up: Assynt

Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.

The croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries. Crofters lived on their crofts and farmed for subsistence, grazing sheep on shared land. Unable to support themselves on the croft alone, most also worked in fishing, kelp, or peat to support themselves.

It was a very hard life. But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way. He is one of just over a thousand residents of Assynt, who chose to stay and continue the crofting tradition.

“I regard the croft as an extension of who I am as a person,” MacAskill explains.

The small community of Assynt. Photo: Screenshot

MacAskill introduces us to some of the other members of the community. Anna is a sheepdog owner and trainer, whom we see herding sheep using the same techniques people here have used for centuries. Stuart is a passionate fisherman, who shares his love of Assynt’s natural landscape with his young son.

We also meet some of the creatives who have, MacAskill says, been drawn by the unique landscape and material culture. We see a potter using local materials, a fiddler, and a spinner on her spinning wheel.

The spinning wheel came to Europe from the Middle East by the 13th century, and was widely adopted by the 18th century, replacing the older drop spindle and distaff. Photo: Screenshot

MacAskill moved to the croft a decade ago, and doesn’t regret it. Having grown up visiting every summer, he has always felt drawn to the land and knows others feel the same. But a small, isolated community like Assynt is constantly in danger of depopulation. MacAskill hopes that people keep choosing to move back and stay, heeding the same call he did.

The film ends on this note, with a montage of scenes from life in Assynt and the landscape it sits in, while an elderly crofter sings a traditional Scottish song of homecoming.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8261. Day 32: Shifting From Solitude to the Familia Real

My desire to walk under the stars had diminished. Not because I didn’t love it or miss it, but because my body was in desperate need of rest.

So I began my day in the light of dawn, the clouds a wispy presence intertwining with the mountains outside of Ponferrada.

The road leading out of the city were adorned with the colors of fall.

Fiery reds, mustard yellows, vibrant greens.

At 10 am, I reached the 200 km from Santiago sign. A man was set up next to it, selling wax stamps. As I neared the end of the road, the stamps had become more elaborate. The pilgrim passport book helped document the journey for the credentialing process at the end, but it was also a time capsule for us to look back on this journey. At least I knew I would.

While I strolled along during the picture-perfect autumn day, I listened to a playlist my Italian brother made for my full moon walk. It solely contained the peaceful melodies of Ludovico Einaudi. The piano and walking put me into a trance.

Walking alone that day, I noticed a shift within myself since the full moon walk.

The Camino had gifted me such great friends. The journey was nearing its end, and with that, the moment of saying goodbye.

I’d still enjoy my moments of solitude, but it was no longer my priority. My priority was savoring every last drop of what was around me, especially the people I’d gotten so close with.

Immediately after I wrote that, I walked up on my Italian brother lying on a bench, soaking up the sun. I threw off my pack and copied his idea. He pulled out a pastry that he bought for me—chorizo wrapped in dough—and I was in heaven.

We strolled up and down hills, surrounded by the vineyards and mountains around us. He played Latino music and danced, which is the exact energy I needed to feed off of.

We arrived in the mountain town of Villafranca del Bierzo and went to an albergue that multiple pilgrims recommended: Ave Fénix Pilgrims Hostel. As soon as we arrived, I knew why it was recommended. The main entrance, where we checked in, was made of old wooden beams, stone, and plaster. A wood stove and meat drying from the ceiling created a comfortable and rustic atmosphere. It felt like an old Spanish man’s cabin that he welcomed pilgrims into.

When I got to my bunk, I immediately fell asleep.

The brief nap was exactly what I needed to spend the rest of the evening with both of my brothers.

In conversation, the topic of nail polish got brought up, and we agreed on the color white to paint each of our nails. For all three of us, that color symbolized a unique aspect of ourselves. So with their surprising willingness, we set out into the town to make it a reality.

On the way, the brothers each bought a chorizo bocadillo to snack on while we walked. They each passed the sandwich to me, knowing I’d want a bite, and we found a local woman to point us in the right direction for nail polish. Back at the albergue, we each painted a few nails white. Just another way to showcase the bond that was built between us.

I’d given the three of us the name “Familia Real.” I’d experienced trail families in the past, but this felt different, deeper in a way.

The albergue we stayed in had a donativo dinner, and all the feelings I had about the location began to make sense. Jesús, the owner of the property and supposed legend of the Camino, was an old man who made an appearance. He shook hands with each of us as he walked past and told one pilgrim in Spanish,

“I built this place stone by stone with my hands.”

Before we began eating, he had us all stand, take hands, and raise them above our heads before saying a blessing over us that felt different than the others I’d received. He called upon the four elements and wished health to the pilgrims on their way to Santiago. As we passed around the spaghetti prepared by the volunteers, Jesús was adamant that we each served ourselves and no one else.

The intention behind it all felt pure. I could taste the love in the meal.

And with my brothers sleeping in the bunk next to me and some sort of medicinal branches under our mattresses, I went to bed in peace.

#8259. Florida Man Finishes Four Corners Walk Across America

After over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk. His route took him from coast to coast, then corner to corner, starting in Florida and ending in Maine, where a crowd of supporters met him last week.

Kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida. After struggling with drug addiction, mental illness, and the justice system during his early adulthood, he decided to become an endurance athlete and mental health advocate. On January 1, 2022, he began his walking project from the beach in Jacksonville.

Over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific. His plans expanded, and he undertook the challenge of walking to all four corners of the contiguous United States. From Long Beach, he headed to the northwesternmost point, Cape Flattery, also in Washington. After trekking south to San Diego, the next corner he headed for was all the way back in Florida, the southeast extremity.

Along the way, Edwards posted frequently on social media about his journey and his recovery from mental illness.

On October 25, Edwards reached West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec, Maine. This is the northeast corner of the U.S., and the finish line for Edwards. He walked a total of 19,544 kilometers in 1,022 days, averaging nearly 20km per day.

Edwards and supporters at the finish line. Photo: Kyndal Ray Edwards

A cross-country walking journey, Edwards says, has been his dream since 2013. But with the end of his Walking Across America project, Edwards is already ruminating on future challenges. Online, he has proposed going on an adventure with a stranger in all 50 states, running more ultra marathons, and undertaking endurance challenges on every continent. However, he has yet to commit to one.

The end of Kyndal Ray Edwards’s journey came only days before Karl Bushby, another long-distance trekker, completed his 28-year Goliath Expedition. The pair also happen, Edwards pointed out, to share a birthday.

#8256. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock. Her fiancé then lost his footing while trying to reach her.

A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair. Using ropes, slings, carabiners, and climbing harnesses, the group formed a human chain to reach both stranded hikers and pull them to safety.

The Electric Arms Race Has Gone Too Far: Tim Shuff questions the growing use of electric motors in outdoor adventure. He argues that the speed and convenience they create undermine traditionally self-propelled activities like paddling and cycling. Today, you can even buy battery-powered SUPs.

While recognizing that electric assistance can make outdoor sports more accessible, he thinks that its wider use will change wilderness areas, reshape trails, and create pressure to build increasingly powerful equipment.

Jan Spicka descends from Huascarán Sur. Photo: Matej Zak

A Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain: Climbing Peru’s Huascarán Sur turned into a tragedy for a group of five friends last July. Czech alpinist Jan Spicka describes how he and partner Matej Zak reached the 6,768m summit before he plunged into a hidden crevasse on the descent.

Matej’s quick reactions saved his life, but their three friends, Saul Mendoza, Chicho Ugarte, and Arti Salas, disappeared while attempting to descend by a different route. With no official mountain rescue in Peru, friends and volunteers pitched in. After 24 hours in the freezing conditions, they knew it was unlikely they would see their friends again. GPS tracks and later searches suggest they had fallen through a collapsing snow bridge.

He Felt Stuck in New York. So He Started Walking to California: Feeling trapped by unemployment and a lack of opportunities in New York, 29-year-old Chantz Rivera began walking across America. He set off with a tent, sleeping bag, and some supplies in a shopping cart. Over 149 days, he walked to California, pushing his cart 32 to 40km a day along highways and through small towns, documenting his progress for his growing number of online followers.

This Mountain Race Makes Runners Carry 60kg of Beer and Supplies Uphill: Slovakia’s annual Sherpa Rallye is one of the world’s unique mountain races. Competitors have to haul heavy loads of supplies up a 5.7km rocky trail to a remote hut in the High Tatras, nearly 2,000m above sea level.

Men carry 60kg, including a 30-liter keg of beer, while women carry 20kg, with the loads secured to wooden frames. The race was started in 1985 by mountain porter Viktor Beranek. The event brings together the region’s nosiči (traditional mountain porters) and also helps stock the remote hut ahead of winter.

A Hiker Slid Hundreds of Meters Down Mount Timpanogos: A female hiker was seriously injured after slipping off the trail near the summit of Mount Timpanogos in Utah. She slid several hundred feet down the steep mountainside before landing on a narrow cliff ledge. Newly released helicopter footage shows her being hoisted to safety. She was taken to hospital and is reportedly recovering.

We Need to Move Past the ‘Shut Up and Die Like a Man’ Mentality in the Mountains: Climber and paraglider Will Gadd reflects on the psychological impact of mountain accidents. Climbing culture often glorifies the dangers people face in the mountains while discouraging them from admitting they are struggling.

Gadd discusses the deaths of two close friends and challenges the underlying expectation that climbers should simply suck it up and carry on. After decades in the mountains, he has seen that the consequences of an accident extend far beyond the immediate incident, affecting survivors and their families and friends for years.

Two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia: Two hikers, identified as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, have died in a suspected grizzly attack near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Their bodies were found during a search after the pair were reported missing by their family.

This comes just a year after a separate grizzly attack in the same area severely injured four people, including three children. The trail remains closed as authorities continue their investigation.

#8254. Supreme Court Clears Way for Border Wall Construction in Big Bend National Park

The US Supreme Court issued an unsigned decision on Monday allowing the Trump administration to resume building border barriers and installing surveillance equipment in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas, including inside Big Bend National Park.

The ruling lifts a temporary halt on construction ordered in early October by US District Judge Kathleen Cardone in El Paso. While litigation over the legality of the 500-mile border project continues in the lower courts, construction crews can now move forward with work. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented from the decision.

For visitors and locals in the remote desert region, the physical ramifications of the project began appearing over the summer. In August, construction crews brought bulldozers near Santa Elena Canyon (one of Big Bend National Park’s most famous landmarks) and graded more than a mile of land. According to administration officials, Customs and Border Protection plans to install four- to six-foot-tall vehicle barriers, surveillance gear, and an access road in the area.

Opponents of the construction, which include a bipartisan mix of Texas ranchers, local landowners, and conservationists, warn that barriers will permanently alter the desert. Critics say the project threatens to cut off access to the river, disrupt livestock and crops, and interfere with the area’s status as the largest dark sky reserve on the planet.

Legal opposition to the project began in April when a coalition consisting of an environmental organization, a river guide, a church preservation group, and local landowners filed a lawsuit to stop the project. The coalition argued that federal officials had exceeded their authority by waiving environmental and conservation laws, such as the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act, without approval from Congress.

In early October, Judge Cardone temporarily blocked the construction after finding that the coalition was likely to succeed on at least one of its legal claims. After Judge Cardone denied the administration’s request to pause her order during an appeal, the government filed an emergency application with the Supreme Court, describing the lower court’s block as “baseless.”

The federal government argued that halting work would leave a gap of more than 300 miles in border defenses, which he said could draw cartels and other bad actors.

Still, the coalition urged the justices to keep the block in place. They argued the administration sought emergency relief to immediately restart bulldozing, blasting, and road building across an ecologically and culturally sensitive landscape, warning that continued work would permanently damage historic resources and private ranch lands.

In Monday’s order, the Supreme Court majority acknowledged the plaintiffs’ argument that construction in the Big Bend Sector would “diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area.” However, the majority concluded that federal law grants the Homeland Security secretary the power to waive conservation and environmental statutes, noting that the law shows “a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms” cited by the challengers.

The decision marks the first major policy victory for President Trump at the Supreme Court following last week’s midterm elections, as the underlying lawsuit proceeds in the lower court.

#8253. Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

Here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27. There will be more, as a few still scramble to raise the money or choose to keep their plans to themselves until the last minute. Because of the long charter flights, an expedition to Antarctica, even a “tourist” Last Degree trip, costs close to $100,000 — more, if you want to do something unusual. These are the journeys announced so far. Skiers hit the ice later this month.

Hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers. Skiers need to travel around 1,130km, averaging around 20km per day.

Brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole. Lumb previously completed a crossing of Norway’s Finnmarksvidda with guiding company Ousland Colliard.

Indian Neeraj Choudhary also trained with Ousland Colliard, crossing the Greenland Ice Sheet in 2024. He hopes to become the second Indian to ski solo and unsupported to the South Pole, following Satish Gogineni, who became the first in 2024-2025.

Satish Gogineni at the South Pole in 2025. Photo: Satish Gogineni

American Lucas Czarnecki will also ski solo and unsupported and claims he will livestream every moment of his journey: “What sets South Signal [his expedition name] apart from other polar expeditions is my commitment to bringing you along for every moment of this extreme adventure. Each day, I will be live-streaming my experience directly from the ice, sharing the raw reality of life on the polar plateau.”

Another American, Meghan Buchanan, will also tackle the route. She plans to start early, leaving for Antarctica on November 12.

Finally, German Dirk Langer will also attempt the route unsupported.

A Berkner Island start means a few extra kilometers, with skiers required to cover around 1,400km to the South Pole.

Max Worsley of the UK and Martin Nesse of Norway also plan to start in early November, but from the edge of Berkner Island. Max is the son of Henry Worsley, who died following an Antarctic expedition in 2015-2016. Max intends to follow much of his father’s final route.

At least two expeditions will begin at the Messner start, 911km from the South Pole. James Garnett of the UK and Norwegian Marius Rehn will each ski solo and unsupported.

Satish Gogineni will be back in Antarctica this year, hoping to build upon his Hercules Inlet experience. Gogineni’s 2026 plan is more ambitious: a solo, 2,000km journey from the outer edge of the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf to the inner edge of the Ross Ice Shelf via the South Pole. Gogineni is billing this as a “world-first human achievement” and the “longest solo traverse ever completed on the Antarctic continent.”

If successful, his route would indeed be longer than the truncated crossings of Colin O’Brady and Lou Rudd in 2018. However, his distance would still be well short of Borge Ousland’s 1997 expedition. Ousland became the first person to cross Antarctica solo and unsupported, though he occasionally used a rudimentary handheld kite known as a ski sail. Ousland skied for 65 days and covered 2,845km. At the time, sails were not considered “support.”

Last year, O’Brady tried a significantly longer expedition than his 2018 effort, attempting to ski from the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf to the tip of Berkner Island on the edge of the Ronne Ice Shelf, a total distance of over 2,800km. He eventually ended his crossing attempt after 100 days, with roughly 40% of his total distance remaining.

A map by PECS (the Polar Expeditions Classification Scheme) showing previous solo Antarctic crossing routes. Photo: PECS

Gogineni’s main challenge might be the weight of his sled. With so much weight spread over two sleds, O’Brady was forced to double carry in soft snow on the Ross Ice Shelf last year. A double carry involved shuttling half of his gear forward, then returning to pick up the rest. This meant he had to cover 15km for every 5km of progress. Gogineni says his sled will weigh 181kg.

Mardi Philips, Ida Olsson, and Nia Owens are calling themselves the Antarctic Valkyries and aim to become the “first all-female team to reach the South Pole of Inaccessibility.” They will start at Thorshammer Station (a spot near the Russian Novolazarevskaya Station in Queen Maud Land) and plan to kite-ski 2,500km, first aiming for the Pole of Inaccessibility (the middle of the Antarctic continent), and then continuing to their finish point at the South Pole.

The Antarctic Valkyries proposed route. Photo: Antarctic Valkyries

A Spanish scientific expedition will cross Antarctica by a new route in a unique wind-powered vehicle.

Part of the wind-sled involves a series of tents. Photo: La Vanguardia

Their “wind-sled ” is 15m long and consists of four modules. It is propelled using 20 kites of various sizes. The largest kite measures 150m² and the smallest 5m². The four-man team plans a 3,400km, 85-day journey from near Novolazarevskaya Station to the Italian research station Concordia, known as Dome C, on the Antarctic Plateau.

The wind-sled team’s proposed route. The green return route is planned for a future expedition. Photo: La Vanguardia

Meanwhile, three Argentine kayakers are preparing to paddle roughly 900km along the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula, from Argentina’s Esperanza Base to San Martín Base. Diego Linares, Juan Tomaselli, and Javier Siede will start their journey in January and plan to spend 30 to 40 days on the water.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8250. A Risky Summit Push on Everest

It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest. Andrey Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have set off for the summit without oxygen, hoping the weather will hold. They are completely alone on the mountain, and the push is full of risk.

Everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m. That was their highest point during their earlier venture in October.  In addition, the wind may rise dramatically on Thursday, Vitor Baia, a Portuguese high-altitude meteorologist, told ExplorersWeb.

“It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.

The question is exactly when the wind will increase, and whether the climbers will have enough time to summit and descend to a safer altitude.

“They have three days of weak wind, until Wednesday [November 11], but then the wind will increase sharply,” said Baia.

He says the best summit day will be Tuesday, with clear skies and weak winds. “Then they could use Wednesday to descend,” he added. “[That day will have] some clouds but still acceptable wind speeds.”

The situation will worsen remarkably on Thursday, when the wind will shift from the west to the northwest and increase dramatically to 50 kph at 8,000m and 60kph at the summit.

In addition, avalanche hazards are still high due to the large amounts of snow after the latest storm two weeks ago. Finally, as winter approaches, it’s getting colder every day, the climbers reported.

After their first trip up ended in a tactical retreat as the cyclone hit, they retreated to Kathmandu to recover from some health issues. Now they are fit again and ready for a second try. They returned to Base Camp last Thursday. Not surprisingly, they found it covered in a thick new layer of snow. Breaking trail, they sank at some points up to their waists, Vasiliev reported.

“Our high-altitude boots were in a cache two hours ahead of us, so we used duct tape to seal our pant cuffs to our trekking boots, trying to keep the snow out,” Kondrashkin reported. They eventually reached the cache and continued up in an exhausting 14-hour-long effort to a second cache (their Camp 1), where they had left their tent and sleeping bags.

They were near an avalanche-prone area and several snow slides swept nearby, prompting them to wait a day before continuing. Meanwhile, Shipilov showed signs of food poisoning. Kodrashkin recalls that Saturday morning started with the following conversation:

“Vitalya, how are you feeling? Are we heading up?”

That answer needs some clarification. A professional like Vitaly Viktorovich [Shipilov] really only has two modes: “We’re going” and “I’m dying.”

In fact, Shipilov had a fever and acute pain in the lower back, so the team headed down to their base in Lobuche. As this was going on, the snow had time to sluff off from the previously avalanche-prone area.

After just one night of rest, Vasiliev confirmed they were going up again. If all went according to plan, they will spend tonight back in their tent above the Lho La. Unfortunately, the climbers have not shared their tracker showing their current location and progress. On their previous trip up, they reached some 7,500m on Everest’s West Shoulder, near the beginning of the West Ridge and the potential detour to the Hornbein Couloir.

Everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Sergey Kondrashkin

#8247. Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Announced

The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been announced.

The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

In addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

The best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush said, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”

In the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

The Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

Directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

The Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”

There were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

For best feature film, the competition announced Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

Director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” said Kerry Stauffer.

Last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

Tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently announced Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

#8243. A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”

Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

The first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

From there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he says the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka plans to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

#8241. CDT Trail Town Warns Hikers of Suspected Rat Poison on Local Trails

Authorities in the CDT trail town of Helena, Montana are warning the public that suspected rat poison has been discovered on trails in the area. Hikers and locals are being asked to keep a close eye on the ground while hiking local trails, especially if accompanied by dogs.

In a recent Facebook post, Helena police described the suspected poison as small, green tablets. Authorities say that accidentally ingesting the tablets poses a serious health risk, particularly to pets and small children.

For day hikers and trail runners who visit the CDT near Helena with their dogs and families, police urge extra caution and close supervision.

The first incident reportedly occurred on October 6th, when an individual reported finding a small quantity of the suspected rat poison on a local trail. With no information on a suspect or additional reports, several weeks passed with no updates.

However, over the weekend, police announced that more of the suspected poison has surfaced across multiple trails in the Helena vicinity.

If you come across small, green tablets or any other suspicious substances while hiking, do not touch them, keep your pets and children away from the area, and contact the Helena Police Department immediately to report the location.

#8240. Matt Robertson Just Won $1.25 Million In the Champions Tournament. It’s The Largest First Place Payout in Professional Bass Fishing History

Published Oct 31, 2026 6:48 PM EDT

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

With a final day tally of 20 pounds, 2 ounces, and a total 3 day weight of 56 pounds and an ounce, Matt Robertson won a first-place payout of $1.25 million in the Champions bass fishing tournament on Old Hickory Lake in Tennessee. This is the largest first-place payout in the sport’s history and it represents an interesting turn in pro bass fishing.

Before we dive into the rest of the results, here’s what you need to know about the tournament and how it all came together.

It’s been just over 8 years since the professional bass fishing world effectively split the best anglers in the world into two separate organizations, the Bassmaster Elite Series and the MLF Bass Pro Tour. In that time, new names have risen to the top of the leaderboards, and the old guard has won their fair share of events as well.

But the question that seemed to circulate year after year was who really is the best angler in the world?

Since the two organizations don’t cross-compete well, the answer remained shrouded in speculation and uncertainty. Sure, Jacob Wheeler might be the best at catching the most fish under the MLF BPT format, but could he still sack up 5 giants for 4 consecutive days in an Elite Series format? Would the young gun, Trey McKinney, give Wheeler or Kevin VanDam a run for their money in an MLF-style event?

The bass fishing world figured we’d never know, that is, until February of this year when World Bass Enterprises introduced The Champions Tournament. CEO Brian Bird announced the tournament, and an eye-popping $3.25 million purse to go along with it. Bass fishing fans from around the world started to pay attention.

To qualify for The Champions Tournament, Bassmaster Elite Series anglers and MLF Bass Pro Tour anglers fished their respective 2026 tours throughout the year. After each event, they were awarded Angler of the Year points. The Champions Tournament lineup consisted of the top 25 in AOY points from the Elite Series and the MLF Bass Pro Tour. The additional spots were filled based off of a “win and you’re in” ruling that applies to anglers who won one of the major events, but didn’t make the points cut.

Two additional anglers were selected through a random draw that WBE put on for those who pre-ordered the Pay-per-view streaming service.  Due to naming rights, the anglers were split into teams. Elite anglers were assigned ‘Team Stars’ and MLF Bass Pro Tour anglers were assigned ‘Team Stripes’. The two randomly drawn anglers are Eric Giessing (Stars) and Kyle Carr (Stripes).

At the end of the event, a trophy was awarded to the top performing team, also “settling” the debate of which organization has the better anglers. For the 2026 Champions Tournament, Team Stars (Elite Series) has won bragging rights for the year.

“There has always been friendly competition and banter between the anglers on each tour, but no way to actually settle the score on the water,” MLF Bass Pro Tour 2025 Angler of the Year Jacob Wheeler said in a statement. “The opportunity to crown a true world champion across the entire sport is something our anglers have wanted for a very long time.”

The Champions Tournament was held on Old Hickory Lake, launching out of Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tennessee. The launch and respective FanFest was full of attractions like a petting zoo, kids fishing area, inflatable archery, cornhole tournament, boat demos, and more. They even had the legendary Bill Dance fire off a cannon during the shotgun launch on the first day of competition.

Unsurprisingly, forward-facing sonar was addressed for this event, and seemingly played into a 50/50 outcome. For the first two days of competition, anglers were able to select which day they’d fish with live sonar, and which day they’d go without it. Then for the top 15 anglers fishing the final day, they got to use live sonar for 3 hours of competition.

To add to the pomp and circumstance, as if $1.25 million wasn’t enough, the weights also reset for the top 15 anglers heading into the final day. Making it truly anyone’s ballgame coming into Saturday. Old Hickory Lake put on quite a show for the first two days of competition, with largemouth, spotted bass, and smallmouth all making their way to the scales. The smallmouth dominant bags carried the most weight due to the minimum keeper size being 18-inches, while largemouth and spotted bass only needed to be 14-inches to make the cut.

The final day featured the following anglers fighting for the first place prize.

Matt Robertson, Ron Nelson, Bob Downey, Fisher Anaya, Pake South, Jason Christie, Trey Mckinney, Takahiro Omori, Kyle Welcher, Cole Sands, Chris Johnston, Cody Meyer, Bryan Thrift, Michael Neal, and Wesley Strader.

And while they all certainly wanted the top prize, the second place through seventh place payouts weren’t anything to scoff at either. Here is a look at the top 7 anglers, their final day weights, and their payouts after the final weigh-in. 15th place made a cool $20,000 and the payouts increased in $5,000 increments up to 7th.

1st Place: Matt Robertson (20-02) — $1.25 Million

3rd Place: Wesley Strader (11-02) — $300,000

4th Place: Trey Mckinney (11-0) — $200,000

5th Place: Michael Neal (10-10) — $100,000

While we put the largest professional bass fishing payout ever in the rearview mirror, it’s worth considering what The Champions Tournament means for bass fishing fans everywhere. Personally, there’s a bit of a shock factor involved. The payouts for the Bassmaster Classic and MLF Redcrest combined don’t even sniff the purse that was just awarded during this three-day event. That’s truly awe inspiring.

But what it really has shown me is that the two major organizations need to do some soul searching. If World Bass Enterprises can come out of nowhere and pull this off, perhaps it’s time to look at how they were able to do it successfully. Would fans pay a yearly subscription to watch a Pay-per-view Elite or BPT event? If so, could that increase the purses for those events and help the professionals in our sport actually make a living? I don’t see why not.

I know change is difficult for outdoorsmen and women, it’s in our nature to hold on to traditions and the status quo, but this weekend has shown me that there is a way to actually grow the sport of competitive bass fishing in a meaningful way. Now we’ll see if either organization actually has the guts to give it a try and truly make their anglers’ lives better.

As a final thought, I was blown away by the live coverage and the fanbase that showed up in-person and online, especially with the seasonality of this event. The bass fishing world was hungry for The Champions Tournament, and World Bass Enterprises pulled it off in epic fashion. I’m already looking forward to the 2027 lineup.

#8237. First Ski Descent of Meru Central

Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

“Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

The three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

The icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein

The icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

At the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein

The skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

“We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

Tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

#8234. Here’s What Most Hunters Get Wrong About Whitetails, According to a Top Deer Expert

Published Nov 1, 2026 10:14 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Jeff Sturgis has the unique experience of living through dozens of deer seasons all at once. As the founder of Whitetail Habitat Solutions, he works with clients around the country to improve their deer hunting and private land habitat.

But before ever stepping foot on a property, Sturgis does in-depth interviews with these hunters to understand what they’d like to improve and what problems they’ve been having. Through this process, trends start to emerge.

Sturgis calls these problems “huntisms.” But they could also be described as misconceptions, misunderstandings, or straight up bad information. Whatever you want to call them, there are certain things that hunters get wrong when it comes to hunting mature bucks and managing habitat for those mature bucks.

So in this episode of the Outdoor Life Podcast, Sturgis will reference his decades of experience working on private land habitat as well as his time spent hunting on public ground to outline the most common and detrimental deer hunting mistakes. Heed his advice for a better season next year.

This common mentality of having to pound the woods and hunt all the time has saved a lot of big deer over the decades, Sturgis says.

“In some cases I can see this being partially true,” Sturgis says. “Maybe if you’re hunting public land, you’ve got ten spots and you’ve got the time to hunt freely.”

But if you’re hunting small parcels where you can’t afford to spook deer, then it’s usually smarter to stay home when hunting conditions are poor in order to not burn out your stands.

“There’s something to be said for minimizing your hunting, taking care of other priorities in life and expecting a higher rate of potential success because you’ve not over-pressured your stand locations.”

“It’s not just your stand locations [that you don’t want to burn out, it’s also your family, your career, your friends — it extends to an entire way to look at things. When I go out in the woods I want there to be a reasonable expectation that I’m going to shoot a deer for this reason.”

Sturgis says that if you have a “rutcation” planned where you know you’re going to hunt for a solid seven to nine days in a row, then it’s critical to reduce your impact. Instead of charging into a core area regardless of conditions, hunt spots where your scent cone won’t spook deer (because it’s blowing over a lake or off a cliff). And when conditions aren’t ideal, hunt transition areas where you could catch a big buck walking by, but you won’t spook deer near bedding areas or primary food sources.

Sturgis works with many clients who have the financial resources to grow and maintain sprawling food plots on their properties. Many of these clients believe that growing the maximum amount of food on the property will translate to holding the most amount of mature bucks in the fall.

But that’s not how it plays out most of the time. Growing too much summertime food — like big clover or bean plots — will increase the number of does and fawns on the property. During the summer and early fall, mature bucks don’t like to live on crowded food sources and bedding areas, Sturgis says.

“When you add summer food to good cover, you get a lot of does and fawns,” Sturgis says. “And those does and fawns that are here today are here to stay.”

These deer take up space and resources. Mature bucks will live on the fringes of these high-density deer areas but not establish a core zone there.

“Yeah, some bucks will come through during the rut. But bucks, the older they get, they don’t want that commotion and stress of a bunch of does and fawns. That’s why they live somewhere else.”

Sturgis says it’s better to focus on a comprehensive management strategy with proper deer cover, screening cover, sanctuaries, water holes, fall food, and yes, maybe some summer food plots, than it is to simply plant clover plots throughout the entire property.

“If you want to raise the population, add summer food. If you want to lower the population, get rid of summer food,” Sturgis says. “When I go to a client and see 20 acres of beans on their 200-acre property and we drive around and see over 100 does and fawns and only a couple bucks, they have a severe problem. I’d rather have those does and fawns be somewhere else in the summertime and shift over to the property starting in September and October.”

Don’t read this as an attack on food plots. Sturgis has written countless articles on the benefits of food plots, he’s got an online food plot class, he’s authored a book on the subject, and Whitetail Habitat Solutions sells food plot seed. So yes, food plots can be a critical element in consistently harvesting mature bucks.

But that doesn’t mean you should always hunt over them.

“This year I shot four bucks in four states with my bow … and not one of them was shot on a food plot,” Sturgis says. “Then I go to clients and they’re spending 90 percent of their hunts on food plots — and I’m not saying I never hunt on food plots — but the point is that the vast majority of my bucks are shot not in food plots.”

Sturgis tries to convince his clients to hunt away from food plots. Focusing instead on waterholes or funnels in the woods that might lead to food. This helps hunters spook fewer deer and see target bucks during daylight hours.

“Food plots have the greatest level of potential reward and the greatest level of risk,” Sturgis says. “If you spook out those food plots, you’ve just destroyed your property.”

Even though Sturgis has access to prime whitetail properties in the Midwest, he also hunts public land in Pennsylvania every year. In 22 seasons of hunting the same public area, Sturgis has shot 18 bucks.

It’s pretty common for him to bump into other hunters on these hunts, but he doesn’t sweat it. He just moves somewhere else. The key is being flexible and using tactics that match the conditions. For example, if it’s snowy and windy, Sturgis might still hunt through an area. If the woods are blanketed in crunchy leaves, he’ll opt to sit for the day.

One way that Sturgis makes sure that he avoids other hunters is by walking in at twilight (not in the dark).

“You don’t have to be to your spot before light,” Sturgis says. “When I’m walking into a spot like that, I don’t know what tree I’m going to be sitting under or in… So we’re walking into an area in daylight and still hunting [our way in].”

Read Next: 35 Deer Hunting Tips to Read Before This Season

It’s also important to remember that other hunters will bump deer long distances, not just a few hundred yards.

“Public land deer will get pushed a long way,” Sturgis says. “Especially in open woods. Where we hunt we can get 200-yard shots in the woods in some places. So when people push deer out there, they’re moving three quarters of a mile. So don’t think about just one little thicket. Think about how deer are moving in the big picture [across the landscape].”

#8233. Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories

It was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

“They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” said Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”

Inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

“We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories

#8230. I Shot the World Record Archery Elk While Hunting in Montana’s Belt Mountains

Published Nov 2, 2026 9:46 AM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Imagine yourself in a tree stand in Montana’s Belt Mountains. You know a bull elk is approaching because you’ve heard him bugle several times. The bugles were high-pitched one-tone squeals, indicating an immature bull. You’re after a trophy-class animal, but still you can’t help but get excited and you tighten the grip on your 73-pound compound bow.

A twig cracks behind you. You turn slowly and get the surprise of your life. There, not 30 yards away, stands a monstrous bull elk. His antlers are so massive that you wonder how he can hold up his head. This might be the next world-record elk!

You slowly twist the upper half of your body to your right. Trying hard to control your excitement, you try to draw your bow. You can’t! You’re in such an awkward position and your bow is so powerful that you can’t shoot!

That’s exactly the situation in which Dave Snyder, a Las Vegas fireman, found himself last year. But Snyder was no stranger to the frustrations involved in hunting trophy-size elk. He’d bowhunted the Belt Mountains seven previous times and each time he’d killed an elk. Two of those had been large enough to be listed in the Pope and Young Club record book of bow-killed big game. But this bull was larger than any other he’d seen.

Big-game hunting has been in Snyder’s blood ever since he was 12 years old, when he killed his first deer with an old .25/30 rifle in Nevada. Since he took up bowhunting 20 years ago, he has traveled all over the West in search of game. Among his trophies are an Alaskan moose and caribou, wild boars, bears, whitetail deer, Catalina goats and more mule deer bucks than some hunters see in a lifetime.

But elk hunting has been his first love ever since he killed his first bull, a five-pointer, in Colorado in 1972. From each hunt, he has drawn knowledge that has improved his skills. As he admitted to me last summer, his success at bowhunting elk has not been an accident.

For three years running, he bet friends as much as $500 that he’d kill, with his bow and arrow, a bull elk with at least five points on each antler. He won every time. Now he can’t find anybody to bet with him.

“It might seem pretentious for me to bet like that,” Snyder said, “but it’s really not. I’m just confident. If you know what you’re doing, a bowhunter has just as good a chance as a rifleman of taking a big bull—maybe even a better chance. Most gun hunters do well only if there’s a lot of snow. Bowhunters have the advantage of being able to hunt in September during the rut when elk are most vulnerable.”

Snyder’s Montana elk hunting success started almost by accident in 1974. He and another Las Vegas fireman, Mike Freeman, were having trouble with their truck’s carburetor, so they stopped by the side of the road and opened the hood. Dressed in full camouflage, they soon attracted the attention of a local logger, Dee Hills, who stopped to offer help. Hills had been very successful while rifle hunting for elk, but he was a novice bowhunter and had doubts about the killing power of arrows. Snyder and Freeman assured Hills that, yes, arrows kill elk very effectively.

“Why don’t you show me?” Hills suggested. “I know where the elk are and I’d be happy to take you there.”

After fixing the truck, the three hunters drove to Hills’ hunting area in the Belt Mountains. The next morning they hiked into a deep bowl and found a herd of elk almost immediately. But it wasn’t until afternoon that they got close to the animals. Soon a calf came ambling by Snyder and Hills.

“Aren’t you going to shoot?” Hills asked.

Soon the biggest cow in the herd walked to within 25 yards. Snyder drew his bow, aimed and released the arrow. It was a perfect hit and the animal dashed into the trees.

Snyder stifled a laugh. Hills didn’t understand that most arrow-shot animals streak away for 25 to 200 yards before piling up.

“No, that was a good hit,” Snyder said. “We’ll find her. But this will be a good chance for you to learn how to track.”

Snyder had to eat his words when they followed the cow. A wide trail of blood plainly led to where the elk lay dead only 75 yards from where she had been hit.

During the next few years, Snyder and some of his friends made a tradition of hunting together with Hills. They had remarkable success for bowhunters, something they attribute to careful observation and study.

One afternoon, Hills, Snyder and Larry Crim were fanned out on a ridge when a bull bugled. Snyder trotted directly toward the sound. Soon two bulls began bugling back and forth. Stalking carefully, Snyder soon got to within 40 yards of a small five-point but he guessed that the other bull was bigger by the sound of its voice. Suddenly the big bull bugled again within about 60 yards. Snyder sneaked closer but stopped when he saw several cows feeding. Knowing that herd bulls often circle their harems to keep intruders away, Snyder knelt and waited. Within seconds an exceptional six-point bull appeared, walking directly toward him. When the elk was about 25 yards away, he stopped and looked back toward his cows. Snyder quickly drew and released. The Satellite-tipped arrow smacked into the chest. The bull threw back his head and galloped through a barbwire fence before crashing to the ground. The bull’s antlers scored 357⅞ points with the standard measuring system used by the Pope and Young Club. The rack still ranks No. 17 in the club’s record book.

Most hunters probably would have taken a shot at the five-pointer, ruining their chances for the record-class bull. Snyder well understands the importance of passing up opportunities while trophy hunting. His other elk listed in the Pope and Young records was shot under similar circumstances.

Snyder was watching a big herd of cows when a five-point bull came within 20 yards, offering an easy broadside shot. The elk didn’t seem large enough to keep such a large harem to himself, so Snyder decided to pass up the shot. In seconds, a big six-point streaked around the cows, stopped within bow range and looked at the small bull. Then he looked toward Snyder, who was crouched in some undergrowth. When the elk turned again, Snyder shot. The arrow buried itself in the animal’s lungs. The bull covered less than 50 yards before dropping dead. Its antlers later scored 248⅞. A minimum score of 240 is required for listing in the record book.

Taking two record-book elk might satisfy many hunters but not Dave Snyder. He knew there were elk big enough to break the Pope and Young world record in Montana, a state that yields more truly exceptional bulls than any other. He felt his experience gave him just as good a chance as anybody else to find such an animal.

The Belt Mountains offer ideal habitat. Covered mostly by lodgepole pines, Snyder’s hunting area is broken up by dozens of logging clearcuts where elk find a good supply of the grass and low brush they need. Although the Belts aren’t as rugged and remote as some other elk-rich ranges in Montana, they offer plenty of cover in which crafty old bulls can hide from hunters and attain the old age necessary for growing outsize antlers.

The hunter had learned that elk are much more set in their habits than many sportsmen realize. In 1981, Snyder decided to take advantage of that by hunting from a tree stand near heavy elk sign.

On the first day of the season, Snyder carried a portable tree stand to a drainage about two miles from camp. He’d taken one of his record-book bulls there and had seen larger ones. Partway there, he walked to within 35 yards of an unusual spike bull with antlers at least two feet high. Snyder already had decided to shoot nothing smaller than a six-pointer for the first five days of the season but he was tempted to take the spike. After all, it would yield a freezer full of delicious meat and would make an unusual trophy. He finally decided to hold to his resolution and so watched the spike feed out of sight. But he had second thoughts about doing so.

Snyder set his stand in a tree overlooking a recently used elk wallow and several rubs—small trees had been debarked by elk preparing their antlers for the fighting and breeding season.

The next morning, Snyder rose before dawn, confident that he’d have action. But he couldn’t find the stand in the dark. By the time he finally found it, the sun was high and he decided to return to camp for lunch.

That afternoon, he and another Las Vegas bowhunter, Lynn Williams, decided to glass clearcuts and meadows. After half an hour or so, they saw an unusually large bull in a clearcut about 1½ miles away. The men decided to move closer to study the size of the antlers. By the time they reached the cut about an hour later, the bull was gone.

“I’m coming back here in the morning,” Williams said. “I know he’s a monster and, if he came here once, he’ll come again.”

The next morning Williams returned to the cut, Snyder to his tree stand, and Hills and Crim to a drainage that had yielded four elk in previous years, including Snyder’s biggest bull. The four hunters saw only one spike among them.

“I don’t think the rut has started,” Crim said during lunch. “We might as well hunt deer this afternoon. Elk hunting will be a lot easier after the rut starts anyway because the bulls will be bugling.”

Williams and Hills agreed, but Snyder couldn’t get the big bull out of his mind, so he decided to hunt elk while the others hunted deer. By 3:30 he was in the pines above the cut where he had seen the big elk. The elk sign was encouraging—fresh tracks and droppings and several newly destroyed saplings. Obviously elk had been feeding in the cut during the evenings. Normally, Snyder doesn’t like to hunt in or near feeding areas because the animals are extra-wary there, just as they are in bedding areas. Instead, he finds routes between feeding and bedding grounds and ambushes the animals as they pass. But daylight would soon run out, so he decided to find a good place to hide.

A game trail that led from the trees into the clearcut showed signs of heavy use. A spruce sapling, freshly mangled by a bull elk, stood next to the trail. Snyder happened to glance up. An old tree stand, made of two boards nailed between two trees, overlooked the trail. One board was hanging loose, nailed at only one end.

Snyder took a rope from his camouflage fanny pack, climbed the tree and tied the loose board tight. Gingerly, he put his whole weight on the stand to test it. In half an hour it would be too dark to shoot.

Less than 15 minutes later, he heard a faint bugle. It was more of a one-tone squeal than a bugle—typical of the sounds made by spike or raghorn bulls.

In reply, Snyder blew his own bugle, a simple tubular plastic whistle. The bull answered.

Snyder considered climbing to the ground where he’d have good mobility, but he knew he’d be harder to see 15 feet above the ground and that his scent would be more likely to drift high above the bull’s sensitive nose. The bull bugled again. Snyder bugled back and the elk immediately answered. Knowing that too much bugling can spook elk, he decided to wait for the bull to bugle on his own. A minute or so later, the elk squealed again, probably from within 200 yards.

Apprehensively, Snyder whistled for the third time. Again the bull answered with a high-pitched whistle. Snyder was certain the bull was a small one but he decided to prepare for a shot anyway. The bull bugled again, this time within 100 yards. Soon some limbs broke about 50 yards away and a faint sound of hooves on the ground could be heard. Snyder checked his bow and arrow one last time. The sound of his pulse in his ears made it difficult to hear the approaching bull. He fully expected the animal to offer an easy broadside shot on the trail to his left.

Suddenly, less than 30 yards away, a twig cracked behind him. Turning slowly, Snyder saw a magnificent bull with heavy mahogany antlers walk into the clearcut. Twisting to his right, Snyder started to draw his 73-pound Martin Cougar compound. Because of the awkward angle, he could draw it only partway.

The animal began walking slowly to the left. Snyder realized he’d have to twist back to his original position to shoot. He shifted his weight and the thing he had feared happened—the old tree stand creaked. The bull instantly stopped, swung around and stared right at him. Snyder didn’t dare to move. During that tense instant, another bull bugled no more than 200 yards away. The big elk turned and looked toward the sound and resumed walking to the left. Snyder prepared mentally to take a 25-yard broadside shot.

When the bull was behind some branches, it stopped and bugled the call of a spike elk.

“Come on, baby, just three more steps,” Snyder thought. “Just three more steps.”

The other bull bugled again. For no apparent reason, the heavy-antlered bull turned 180° and began walking back into the woods. This time Snyder drew his bow and then twisted around. He could see the bull between two trees that were perhaps 12 inches apart, so he crouched low to shoot under some branches, judged the distance at 45 yards, aimed and released. The orange aluminum arrow was visible during the first part of its flight but then disappeared. The bull hunched over as though he’d been hit and galloped across the clearcut, kicking up such a great cloud of dust that he was hardly visible as he fled. Moments after the bull disappeared into the trees, Snyder heard a crash. Had the magnificent animal fallen?

Snyder climbed to the ground and looked for blood and tracks. Already there was very little light and he could find no sign that he had hit the animal.

He returned to camp to get help and a Coleman lantern. Finding nobody there, he left a note and returned to his stand. He looked for his arrow or blood and found neither, so he searched a logging road that encircled the area but could find no sign that the animal had crossed it. Right then Crim, Williams and Hills arrived. The four men, carrying lanterns, spread out in a line and walked through the trees where Snyder had heard the crash. They knew they had to find the elk within a few hours or the massive animal’s body heat would ruin the game meat. They’d gone about 50 yards when Hills shouted, “There he is!”

The group walked up to the dead bull in silence. He’d fallen so hard that his antler tines had dug several feet under the sod. The antlers were so massive and his body so huge that the four hunters just stood there staring in awe. Finally Hills broke the silence: “Well, we better get to work or we’ll be here all night!”

To get the antlers out of the ground took the combined strength of all four men. The elk was so heavy that just dressing the carcass and dragging it 100 yards down a grassy slope took from 9 p.m. until 3 a.m.

The hunters decided to try winching the carcass off the ground so that the meat could cool. Fortunately, Williams had a powerful winch on the front of his four-wheel-drive pickup. They threw the winch cable over a branch in a large pine, attached the cable to the antlers and lifted the animal clear of the ground. Hanging this way, the bull looked as big as a full-grown rhinoceros.

Later, the bull yielded 560 pounds of boneless fat-free meat. Snyder estimates that the animal weighed well over 1,000 pounds, even after it had been field-dressed.

Read Next: The Real Story Behind the Casey Brooks Bull, the Pending World Record Elk

The 45-pound antlers were a bonus surprise. Though they had looked huge, none of the hunters had guessed that no bowhunter had ever killed a bigger bull. After a required 60-day drying period to allow for shrinkage, the rack was conservatively measured at 389⅞ points with the measuring system used by the Pope and Young Club.

That exceeded the score of the world-record elk taken by Jay Elmer of Arizona in 1980 (“Back-To-Back Bulls,” OUTDOOR LIFE, November 1981). The actual score verified by a panel of judges at the Pope and Young Club’s award banquet last spring was officially put at 391⅞. Snyder’s bull is now recognized as the world record. Even Dave Snyder should be satisfied with that.

This story was originally published in the November 1983 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8229. Howls, Growls, and Sounds of Hounds

Should you use an external loudspeaker while on trail? The internet has spoken: you should not. Should you use headphones? Conclusions vary, but in general, no. Sometimes the internet provides a good reason, and sometimes just an opinion.

Thru-hiking has its mundane moments. And I don’t just mean road-walks – several years ago, I was bored at least once on the John Muir Trail. A few thousand miles later, even though boredom is still very much a thing, I’m able to zone-out more easily. Unless, that is, I get an earworm. Then, my daydreaming gets interrupted.

It was a cold morning on the PCT. I broke camp, started hiking, and realized I’d left my MP3 player in the side pocket of my tent. Digging it out was too much hassle, so I hiked in silence. I noticed a patch of frost within a patch of shade, and that’s how the earworm gained entry. The song that got stuck in my head was “Frosty the S**wman”, and I’m hesitant to name it because it’s so virulent. The first couple of lines rattled around in my skull for the next ten miles. That was the day I learned that listening to music is a good defense against earworms.

The day after the bear incident, I mentally survived a hot, 15 mile road-walk, and physically survived the high speed dump-trucks on County Highway F. Unsettled weather arrived that night, and when I hit the trail the next day, distant thunder started approaching from the west after 30 minutes. The air remained warm even as the storm eventually passed overhead, but the torrential rain was extremely cold. The trail turned into a stream in some places, and a pond in others. Wet feet, no problem. When my music cut out, that was a problem.

My jacket pocket wasn’t as waterproof as I thought, and I discovered that my MP3 player was completely waterlogged. Despite the water sloshing around inside, I was hopeful it might eventually dry out. I shook out as much water as possible before putting it away.

The MP3 player spent that night inside one of my sleep-socks, on top of my foot, like a penguin egg. I incubated it in my shorts pocket the next day, while hiking the Mondeaux River eskers. There was a minor earworm infestation, but I’ve had worse.

At the beginning of the third day, I made a beeline for the town of Rib Lake. It was a full day of distractions.

At the end of the third day, resurrection! Kind of. The MP3 player was able to play music, even though one of its buttons didn’t work. And its display soon flickered and died. It was stuck in “Shuffle” mode, and had developed a couple of other quirks, but it worked well enough. It defended me valiantly against earworms for the remainder of my thru-hike.

I headed north out of town along Kennedy Street. During the 1.5 mile road-walk, three pickup trucks drove past. Each truck was outfitted with several kennels, and each kennel contained an excited, baying hound. As the noise faded into the distance, I reached the trailhead, headed east, and silence descended. With some background music, of course.

That afternoon, I met hikers Linda and Wendy, who were heading west. They were piecing together the entire IAT by parking a vehicle at each of two trailheads, and hiking from one to the next. I met them again at Wood Lake County Park campground, and they were very hospitable. They let me share their campsite, and that evening, Wendy cooked Gnocchi, Pesto, and Chicken of the Woods (mushrooms that she’d picked that day).

In the morning, after only two miles, I saw the three pickup trucks again, empty this time. They were parked at my first trailhead of the day, and I could hear the hounds’ sounds coming from the direction I needed to go. Whether they were training or hunting, I wasn’t sure. Randomly, my MP3 player chose that moment to select “Dueling Banjos”.

Not really. But it would have been appropriate.

I decided to walk the road for a few miles, heading south. Again, the noise faded into the distance.

Compared to western states, Wisconsin sounds different. This was day 17, and I was still noticing birdsongs I hadn’t heard before. The R2-D2 bird, for example. I’d recently discovered that the creatures snorting at me from afar were White-tailed bucks, who apparently have an excellent sense of smell. Mule deer out west have never snorted at me.

In camp, at sunset, three wolf-packs exchanged howls several miles away. It was the only time on the Ice Age Trail that I heard wolves, so they’re probably no more common in the midwest than the west.

The next day, I hiked north along the west bank of the Wisconsin River, then south along the other side. The Grandfather Falls dam and hydropower plant were interesting, but the subsequent out-and-back was not, at least according to FarOut commenters. I know the IAT is a work-in-progress, but I believe a three mile round-trip with no pay-off is optional for thru-hikers. I skipped it, and immediately started a 10 mile road-walk.

I dodged most of a heavy rain shower by sheltering in the pavilion at Tug Lake County Park, and was dry by the time I reached my campsite, which was, in this case, a shelter. It was my first ever night in one – cozy, even if the neighbors were noisy. I now know that the birds at Dog Lake that night were Sandhill cranes.

The next night, my neighbors were remarkably quiet. At the campsite on the other side of Chain Lake, about 300 yards away, were 16 teenagers and two camp counselors from Milwaukee. It sounded like everyone was fast asleep as soon as the sun went down.

I only hitched once on the IAT, going to Rhinelander. I stayed the night, and tried hitching back mid-morning. There were roadworks on the edge of town, which might be why state route 17 wasn’t very busy. An hour later, I had no takers. I tried Uber, also unsuccessfully, then called a cab. Five minutes later, they picked me up. I was back on trail at midday, and reached a suitable place to camp about five o’clock.

Actually, suitable is an exaggeration. I chose a flat patch of grass beside a five-way intersection of overgrown, disused dirt roads. I wouldn’t have camped there if this had been Grizzly territory.

As expected, the intersection was busy that night, but each disturbance didn’t keep me awake for long. Then, at 1:15 AM, something started growling at me, and I was wide awake in an instant, heart thumping.

I’ve been growled at by dogs and coyotes, and grumbled at by porcupines and raccoons. This sound wasn’t canine, and the animal making it didn’t sound small. In my imagination, the creature was bear-sized.

I used my outside voice, but there was no reaction. I unzipped my tent door and shone my flashlight around. Still no movement. I couldn’t see the animal because it was on the other side of my tent. Periodically, for about 15 minutes, it uttered a low, rumbling growl lasting several seconds. Each time, I replied with a few words.

Then, at last, it padded quietly away. I lay awake for 45 minutes while the adrenaline subsided. In the morning, when I had cell service, I researched my nocturnal visitor, and suddenly everything made sense. Wisconsin is the Badger State.

Fast-forward a few hours, and I had a silent night. Wholly unexciting night. All was calm, all was quite… normal. The morning was a bit chilly, but that’s hardly worth mentioning.

In the afternoon, near the tiny community of Polar, I arrived at my chosen campsite on the shore of Mueller Lake. On the water, I could hear a couple of speedboats, their stereos, and the shrieks of people enjoying themselves. The boaters soon went home, and for a time, it was peaceful.

Then the residents of the lakefront house 400 feet away fired up their megawatt outdoor sound system. For the next three hours, I was treated to a Spotify 70’s selection with commercial breaks. Full-size headphones with noise cancelling would have been useful. Fortunately, the loudspeakers fell silent just before sunset.

So, if someone were to suggest that earbuds disconnect me from the sounds of nature, I’d have to disagree. They don’t disconnect me from man-made sounds either.

Sometimes you’ll hear logging on the IAT.

I've spent most of my trail-time in the western states of the US, but also hiked in Scotland, Canada and New Zealand. I planned on being in the PCT class of 2020, but had to postpone. My 2021 SOBO attempt was interrupted by fires and closures. In comparison, the AZT, CDT, PNT, and IAT were almost problem-free. --Richard, aka "LowRange"
